strengths: Addresses an important and under-addressed problem: complete object removal including associated visual effects such as shadows and reflections, going beyond standard inpainting.

The OBER dataset is a substantial contribution: a hybrid of 2,715 camera-captured pairs and 10,000 simulated pairs, with fine-grained annotations including separate object masks, object-effect masks, RGBA foreground layers, and multi-object scenarios. Table 4 convincingly positions it against RORD, MULAN, DESOBA-v2, and ObjectDrop.

The Object-Effect Attention (OEA) mechanism with the L_mask loss (Eq. 2) provides a clean way to decouple foreground removal from background reconstruction by supervising cross-attention maps with object-effect masks; Figure 6 demonstrates good attention recall (0.97) and qualitatively captures shadow and reflection regions.

The Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) strategy is a simple but effective inference-time trick that leverages the predicted attention map for copy-paste blending, yielding strong PSNR-BG gains (28.00 -> 32.98 in Table 2) and visibly reduced background changes in Figures 7 and 12.

Strong and consistent quantitative results: ObjectClear achieves best PSNR/PSNR-BG/LPIPS/CLIP/ReMOVE on RORD-Val, OBER-Test, and OBER-Wild even when baselines are provided with the more informative object-effect mask, while ObjectClear only uses the object mask.

Comprehensive ablations (Table 2) isolate the contributions of the mask loss, simulated data, and AG Fusion, and a 30-participant user study (Table 5) corroborates the quantitative findings with 84-90% preference.
Demonstrated generality through extended applications (object insertion and movement, Figure 8) and robustness to imprecise user strokes (Figure 13).
Limitations are candidly discussed (Appendix C.5), acknowledging failure modes for overlapping shadows and very large shadow regions.
weaknesses: The core methodological components are largely borrowed: the base model is SDXL-Inpainting, and the cross-attention stacking/visual-embedding design explicitly follows Li et al. [16] (FastComposer/PhotoMaker). The novel technical element is essentially a masked attention-supervision loss plus an attention-guided blending, which is a modest increment over existing techniques.

The simulated data (10,000 samples) is constructed by compositing RGBA foreground objects extracted from only 2,715 camera-captured images onto internet backgrounds. The diversity and realism of this simulated data, and thus how much it genuinely extends the data distribution versus recombining a limited object set, is not quantitatively validated.

Evaluation sets are small: OBER-Test has only 160 image pairs, RORD-Val uses 343 samples, and OBER-Wild (300 images) lacks ground truth, relying on ReMOVE and manual annotation. Small test sets weaken the statistical reliability of the reported metric margins.

The reflection-pair simulation in Appendix B uses the authors' own trained model to produce candidate outputs, from which 50 high-quality images are manually selected for training. This introduces potential circularity and selection bias in the training data.
The design choice of using the first-layer cross-attention map for AGF is stated but not justified or ablated; it is unclear whether this is empirically optimal or arbitrary.
The paper does not report inference time, memory, or parameter overhead relative to baselines, which matters for a practical editing tool built on top of a large diffusion model.

Some comparisons are only meaningful under the specific mask-condition protocol; while the paper evaluates baselines under both object-mask and object-effect-mask settings, it is not entirely clear how baselines were adapted (e.g., prompt/conditioning changes) to receive effect masks, which could affect fairness.

Presentation issues: Figure 1's caption and some table layouts are dense, and the paper relies heavily on the appendix for key details (reflection simulation, insertion/movement), which makes the main text harder to assess standalone.

strengths: The paper introduces OBER, a large-scale hybrid dataset for object-effect removal with 12,715 training samples and two benchmarks, providing paired images, precise object masks, object-effect masks, and RGBA foregrounds; this fills an important gap in publicly available data for shadows and reflections.

The proposed ObjectClear combines an Object-Effect Attention mechanism, which supervises cross-attention maps with object-effect masks, and Attention-Guided Fusion, which uses the predicted attention map to preserve background; both components are technically sensible and are ablated.

Experiments are extensive: comparisons on RORD-Val, OBER-Test, and OBER-Wild under two mask conditions, multiple metrics, component ablation, a user study, and applications to object insertion and movement.
Results are strong: ObjectClear achieves the best PSNR, PSNR-BG, LPIPS, and CLIP in Table 1 and is strongly preferred by users in Table 5, supporting the effectiveness of the approach.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with informative figures such as Fig. 3, Fig. 6, and Fig. 12 that illustrate the framework, attention behavior, and fusion effects.
The dataset construction pipeline is carefully designed, including camera-captured pairs, simulation with flat-background selection, multi-object composition, and reflection-pair supplementation.
The method requires only an object mask at inference, making it practical, and the attention-map visualizations support the interpretation of object-effect removal.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparison is not fully controlled: ObjectClear is fine-tuned on OBER, while the baseline methods are not stated to be fine-tuned on OBER. On OBER-Test, this in-domain training advantage may explain part of the large PSNR gap (e.g., 32.98 vs. 27.42 for the best baseline). A fair comparison should fine-tune baselines on OBER or clearly separate in-domain and zero-shot settings.

The attention map evaluation reports only recall (0.97) and not precision or IoU. Since Attention-Guided Fusion directly uses this map for blending, an over-inclusive attention map could still achieve high recall while harming background preservation or leaving artifacts.

The L_mask loss is a simple mean-difference between foreground and background attention values, which does not enforce spatial alignment. The paper does not specify which cross-attention layers are supervised, how attention maps are normalized, or the loss weight, limiting reproducibility.

The simulated data composites foreground objects with their original shadows and reflections onto arbitrary Internet backgrounds. Although objects are grouped by shadow direction, lighting and reflection consistency are not guaranteed, and the reflection simulation uses self-training plus manual selection of 50 samples, which may introduce bias.

Several experimental details are missing: the threshold used to compute object-effect masks, the optimizer and total loss weighting, the exact 'first-layer' cross-attention map used in Attention-Guided Fusion, and the definition of background regions for PSNR-BG. These affect reproducibility.

The closest related method, ObjectDrop, is not quantitatively compared in Table 1; it is only shown qualitatively in Fig. 7. Since ObjectDrop addresses the same task, a quantitative comparison, if feasible, would strengthen the claim.

Attention-Guided Fusion is essentially a copy-paste of the original background outside the predicted effect region; while effective for background preservation, it may limit the method's ability to handle cases where the background itself should change, such as moving objects or changed illumination.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: complete object removal that includes shadows and reflections while preserving background fidelity.

Introduces the OBERT dataset with fine-grained annotations (object masks, object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds, multi-object and reflection scenarios) and two benchmarks, which could be a useful resource if publicly released.
The proposed Object-Effect Attention (OEA) and Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) are reasonable components, and the ablation study shows that each component contributes to the reported gains.

Experiments are extensive: comparisons on RORD-Val, OBERT-Test, and OBERT-Wild under two mask settings, multiple metrics, a user study, qualitative results, user-stroke robustness, and extensions to insertion/movement.
Quantitative results are competitive, achieving best or near-best PSNR, LPIPS, and CLIP on several benchmarks, and the predicted attention map reaches high recall (0.97).
The limitations section acknowledges failure cases such as overlapping shadows and extremely large shadow regions.
weaknesses: The comparison is not apples-to-apples: ObjectClear is fine-tuned on OBERT with object-effect supervision, while the baselines are not trained/fine-tuned on the same dataset or with the same effect-level supervision. Much of the reported gain may come from the training data and AGF rather than from the proposed method itself; controlled experiments with baselines fine-tuned on OBERT are needed.

PSNR-BG is inflated by the Attention-Guided Fusion strategy: AGF copies original background pixels outside the predicted attention region, so high PSNR-BG and user preference for background preservation are largely by construction, not evidence of better generative inpainting. The main ablation gain is from AG Fusion (28.00 to 32.98 PSNR), suggesting the core attention mechanism contributes modestly.

Reproducibility and usefulness are limited: there is no explicit code or dataset release statement or URL, and key details of OBERT (threshold for object-effect masks, simulation pipeline, reflection-pair generation) are not fully specified. For a dataset contribution, public availability is essential.

Dataset quality is questionable in places: real-image object-effect masks are computed by pixel-wise differences and may be noisy; simulated data rely on crude alpha/shadow-direction compositing; reflection training pairs are generated by the model itself and manually selected, risking self-training artifacts.
Missing comparisons with recent object-removal methods such as OmniPaint and OmniEraser, which are cited in related work but not evaluated. There are also no error bars or significance tests.

Method novelty is incremental: OEA and AGF are straightforward combinations of existing cross-attention supervision and copy-paste fusion ideas. There is no ablation on important design choices, e.g., feeding the original image instead of the masked image to SDXL-Inpainting, which cross-attention layer is used for AGF, or the prompt design.
The OBERT-Wild result is only marginally better than RORem on ReMOVE (0.9172 vs. 0.9157), so the claim of superior performance on all benchmarks is overstated.
Clarity issues: the architecture figure and tables are dense, some notation and training details are insufficient, and ethical/social implications of image-editing tools are not discussed.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: jointly removing a target object and its associated visual effects (shadows, reflections), which prior inpainting/removal methods handle poorly.

Introduces a coherent and technically reasonable framework: Adaptive Target-Aware Attention (ATA) with a cross-attention mask loss L_mask that supervises attention maps using object-effect masks, Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) for inference-time background blending, and Spatially-Varying Denoising Strength (SVDS) to reconcile the DS=0.99/1.0 trade-off. Each component is ablated (Table 2, Figs. 9-12).

The OBER dataset is a substantial and useful contribution: 2,715 camera-captured + 10,000 simulated image pairs, with fine-grained object masks, object-effect masks, and RGBA foregrounds, plus two new test sets (OBER-Test with GT, OBER-Wild without GT). The dataset is claimed to be released publicly and fills a real gap (Table 4).

Strong and broad quantitative evidence: ObjectClear leads on RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OmniEraser-Bench, and MULAN across PSNR/PSNR-BG/LPIPS/CLIP/DINO, and notably does so using only the object mask, while several baselines are given object-effect masks (Table 1). The margin on RORD-Val (e.g., 26.24 vs 24.38 GeoRemover) is meaningful.

Thoughtful fairness controls: Sec. 8.3 re-runs baselines with ground-truth object-effect masks for blending (Table 7), and Table 1 reports both mask regimes, strengthening the claim that gains come from better effect generation rather than from privileged blending masks.

Comprehensive evaluation including a 30-participant user study (Fig. 14), robustness to coarse user strokes (Fig. 15), multi-object removal (Fig. 13), object insertion/movement (Fig. 16), and an efficiency advantage (1.63 s/image vs 9.42 s/image, ~3.7B vs ~12B params).
Clear, well-organized presentation with an extensive appendix; limitations are candidly discussed (Fig. 17), and failure modes (over-/under-removal of interacting shadows) are identified.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is largely compositional: the base is off-the-shelf SDXL-Inpainting, and the main mechanism (supervising cross-attention maps with masks) is closely related to prior attention-guidance/attention-refocusing works. AGF is essentially an alpha-blended copy-paste of the original background, and SVDS is a simple spatially masked denoising-strength heuristic. The paper does not clearly articulate how ATA differs conceptually from existing attention-supervision methods beyond the use of object-effect masks.

The AGF design makes the PSNR-BG metric partially 'free': since background pixels outside the (predicted) object-effect region are copied verbatim from the input, high PSNR-BG is partly a construction rather than evidence of generative background reconstruction. The authors partly mitigate this with the Table 7 experiment, but the headline PSNR-BG gains remain conflated with the blending operation.

Results are not uniformly state-of-the-art: on OBER-Wild, ObjectClear (ReMOVE† 0.8470) underperforms OmniPaint (0.8656), which contradicts the abstract's unqualified claim of 'outperforming prior methods.' This is not acknowledged explicitly, and OBER-Wild uses a modified reference-free metric (ReMOVE†) whose design could favor the proposed blending behavior.

Two of the three main test sets (OBER-Test, OBER-Wild) are constructed by the authors, and the simulated training data is generated by a pipeline that relies on off-the-shelf models (DINO, SAM, Depth Anything V2, Mask2Former). This raises potential distribution/method bias and concerns about the fidelity of derived object-effect masks (obtained from I_gt - I_in thresholds, which can capture misalignment/noise).

The 'Reflection Pair Simulation' uses the authors' own trained model to generate candidates that are then manually filtered and added back to training data (Sec. 7), a self-training loop that could reinforce model biases and is only weakly validated.

Some ablation deltas are small and reported without significance/variance (e.g., Table 2 CLIP differences of 0.0010-0.0027 between settings), making it hard to gauge robustness. Hyperparameters (e.g., DS=0.99 background value, Gaussian blur for the soft mask) appear empirically chosen with limited sensitivity analysis.

Comparison fairness is not fully airtight: OmniEraser is run at 1024 and others at 512 (noted in Sec. 8.2), and no per-baseline tuning details are provided; some baselines may be under-optimized in their default configurations.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: removing not only a target object but also its associated effects such as shadows and reflections while preserving background fidelity. The qualitative comparisons in Fig. 1, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, and Fig. 19 clearly illustrate the practical value.

Introduces OBER, a large-scale hybrid dataset (2,715 camera-captured pairs + 10,000 simulated pairs) with object masks, object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds, and multi-object scenarios. If publicly released as promised, this is a useful resource for the object-removal community.

The proposed ObjectClear framework is technically reasonable and well motivated: Adaptive Target-Aware Attention (ATA) supervises cross-attention maps with object-effect masks, Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) blends generated content with the original background, and Spatially-Varying Denoising Strength (SVDS) handles color consistency and incomplete removal.

Ablation studies support the individual components: Table 2 shows progressive gains from ATA, simulated data, AGF, and SVDS; Fig. 6 shows the ATA attention map achieves 0.97 recall on object-effect regions, and Fig. 9/12/13 provide further qualitative evidence.

Extensive quantitative evaluation is provided across multiple benchmarks: RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, OmniEraser-Bench, OmniPaint-Bench, and MULAN. ObjectClear achieves best or near-best results on most metrics, including PSNR-BG, LPIPS, and CLIP, often while using only the object mask rather than the easier object-effect mask.

The user study (30 participants, 80 quadruples) and additional applications (multi-object removal, user strokes, object insertion and movement) strengthen the practical usefulness of the approach. Efficiency is also favorable: 1.63 s/image at 512x512 on an A100, compared with 9.42 s/image for OmniPaint.

The paper is generally clear, well organized, and includes substantial appendix material on dataset construction, implementation details, additional comparisons, limitations, and extended applications.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is incremental: ATA, AGF, and SVDS are combinations/adaptations of existing ideas such as attention guidance, alpha blending, and spatially varying denoising. The strongest contribution is arguably the dataset and empirical study rather than a fundamentally new removal paradigm.

AGF dominates the ablation gains: PSNR rises from 28.04 to 32.77 when AGF is added in Table 2. Because AGF copies the original background outside the predicted attention mask, it may inflate PSNR-BG and perceptual metrics by preserving background rather than improving generative object-effect removal. Table 7 partially addresses this by giving baselines blending masks, but the concern remains.

Dataset construction has potential quality issues. Object-effect masks are computed by thresholded pixel differences between paired images, which can include misalignment or unrelated changes. The simulated data rely on alpha compositing and manual shadow-direction grouping, and the reflection training pairs are selected from the model’s own outputs on 200 images, introducing self-training/circularity bias.

The broad claim that ObjectClear “outperforms prior methods” is not universally supported: on OBER-Wild ReMOVE' in Table 1, ObjectClear (0.8470) is second to OmniPaint (0.8656). The paper should more explicitly acknowledge this exception rather than implying SOTA across all reported settings.

Evaluation scale and statistical rigor are limited in places. OBER-Test (163 samples), OBER-Wild (302), and RORD-Val (343) are relatively small, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. The attention map evaluation reports only recall (0.97) and not precision/IoU, leaving false-positive attention behavior unclear.

Several implementation details are under-specified, which may hinder reproducibility: how visual tokens are appended to text embeddings in SDXL cross-attention, how the input tuple <z_t, I_in, M_o, c> is formed, the number of visual tokens, layer choices for attention extraction, and loss weighting. Code/model release is not mentioned, and the dataset is only promised to be released.

The main quantitative tables do not compare against ObjectDrop, a relevant prior object-removal dataset/method; only a qualitative comparison is shown in Fig. 7. This weakens the quantitative comparison to prior work, even if the omission is due to dataset availability.

The ablation in Table 2 is performed on a single dataset and does not isolate AGF without ATA or test component generality across RORD-Val/OBER-Wild. The conclusions about individual components would be stronger with broader ablation coverage.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: joint removal of a target object and its associated visual effects (shadows, reflections), which is not solved well by standard inpainting/removal pipelines.

Introduces OBER, a substantial hybrid dataset (2,715 camera-captured counterfactual pairs + 10,000 simulated pairs) with fine-grained object masks, object-effect masks, and RGBA foregrounds. This fills a genuine gap (prior datasets are small, non-public, or lack separate effect masks) and the authors commit to public release, which is valuable to the community.

Broad and convincing empirical validation: SOTA on RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, and, importantly, on three external benchmarks (OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, MULAN in Tables 5-6). The external results materially mitigate concerns about self-evaluation and show the method genuinely generalizes.

Systematic ablations that isolate each component (ATA, simulated data, AGF, SVDS) in Table 2 and Figures 9-12, plus a user study (Fig. 14) and an efficiency comparison (~5x faster than OmniPaint/OmniEraser), supporting the design choices and the practical value.
Clear presentation, informative qualitative comparisons, and a thorough appendix covering mask robustness, object insertion/movement, and limitations (Fig. 17).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. ATA is essentially cross-attention supervision via a simple mask-contrast loss (Eq. 2); AGF is a background copy-paste controlled by a predicted attention map; SVDS is a heuristic DS=1.0/0.99 spatial split. Each component is an incremental combination of known ideas rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The Attention-Guided Fusion step makes background preservation partly self-fulfilling: outside the predicted object-effect region the output is literally the input, so the very large PSNR-BG gains (e.g., 29.78 vs. 24-26 on RORD-Val) are largely achieved by construction. Table 7 (baselines given GT effect masks for blending) partially addresses this, but the headline 'background fidelity' advantage should be interpreted cautiously and is somewhat inflated by design.

The simulated reflection pairs are generated by the authors' own trained model with human-in-the-loop selection and then fed back into training (and the effect category is partly evaluated on such effects), creating a self-training/circularity concern that could bias the reflection results.

Evaluation depends partly on the authors' own test set (OBER-Test, 163 samples) and a self-modified metric (ReMOVE') for OBOR-Wild (302 samples, no ground truth). Small test sets with no variance/statistical-significance reporting weaken the strength of the quantitative claims.

Metric choices are weak proxies for removal quality (PSNR, CLIP feature distance) and the user study is limited in scope; stronger perceptual or human-centric evaluation of the generated object-effect region would better support the 'precise removal' claim.

Minor technical concerns: Eq. 1's alpha map for effect regions, (I_gt - I_in)/(I_gt + eps), can yield negative/undefined values for brightening effects such as reflections unless clamped (no clamp is stated), and key hyperparameters (DS=0.99 background, threshold for effect masks) are described only as 'empirical' without justification.
